sources.title: Predicting Affect Classification in Mental Status Examination Using Machine Learning Face Action Recognition System: A Pilot Study in Schizophrenia Patients
sources.locator: Methods and Results: five senior psychiatrists rating recorded seven to ten minute interviews with 25 male inpatients; mean inter-rater agreement of 54% for affect quality, 43% for range, and 25% for subtype; Discussion paragraph on heterogeneity of affect rating and on the distinction between mood and affect; stated limitations
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY 4.0) as displayed on the article page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the reported inter-rater agreement percentages, the study's sample and interview length, its stated limitations, and its restatement of the conventional distinction between a sustained internal reported mood and an observed changeable affect. No wording, figure, table, or organisational structure was reused; the lesson's explanation, case, and examples are its own.

agentAccess.notes: This project's source-access ledger records pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov as allowed because its robots file carries Allow: /articles/, which is the route used. No login, paywall, rate limit, or technical control was bypassed.

sources.title: Do Words Matter? Stigmatizing Language and the Transmission of Bias in the Medical Record
sources.publisher: Journal of General Internal Medicine, Society of General Internal Medicine
sources.locator: Methods: randomised vignette design, 413 medical students and residents, two chart notes describing the same hypothetical 28-year-old man with sickle cell disease; Results: attitude score 20.3 versus 25.1 on a 7 to 35 scale and resident pain-management score 4.7 versus 5.3 on a 2 to 7 composite; Methods description of the three features that made the note stigmatising
sources.license: Copyright Society of General Internal Medicine 2018; used here only as a factual reference

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the study design, sample, and reported numeric outcomes, and for the bounded fact that the stigmatising note cast doubt on the patient's pain, added irrelevant markers of lower socioeconomic status, and implied uncooperativeness. Neither vignette note, nor any scale item, table, or sentence, was reproduced or adapted; the lesson's own notes about R. are original.

agentAccess.notes: Retrieved through the PMC articles route that this project's source-access ledger records as allowed by robots. The publisher's own site was not accessed. No login, paywall, or technical control was bypassed.

sources.title: Physician Use of Stigmatizing Language in Patient Medical Records
sources.publisher: JAMA Network Open, American Medical Association
sources.locator: Methods: 600 randomly selected ambulatory internal-medicine encounter notes written by 138 physicians in 2017 at one urban academic centre; Results: the five categories of negative attitude, namely questioning credibility, disapproval, stereotyping, portraying the patient as difficult, and unilateral decision making
sources.license: Copyright 2021 Park J et al.; open access under the CC-BY License as displayed on the article page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the study's setting and sample and for the names of the five recurring categories of negative expression, together with the bounded fact that credibility is questioned through markers such as 'claims' and 'insists' and through quotation marks. No quoted chart excerpt from the study, and no table, figure, or passage of its text, was reproduced or adapted.

agentAccess.notes: Retrieved through the PMC articles route recorded as allowed in this project's source-access ledger. No login, paywall, rate limit, or technical control was bypassed.

sources.title: Examination of Stigmatizing Language in the Electronic Health Record
sources.publisher: JAMA Network Open, American Medical Association
sources.locator: Methods: cross-sectional analysis of 48,651 admission notes for 29,783 patients written by 1,932 clinicians at one urban academic medical centre in 2018, using condition-specific word lists; Results: 2.5% of notes carried at least one stigmatising descriptor, and the adjusted difference for Black compared with White patients was 0.67 percentage points (95% CI 0.15 to 1.18)
sources.license: Open access under the CC-BY License as displayed on the article page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the study's setting, note count, the overall prevalence figure, and the adjusted difference with its confidence interval, plus the bounded fact that the count rested on lists of descriptors such as 'refused' and 'noncompliant'. No word list, table, figure, or passage of the article was reproduced or adapted.

agentAccess.notes: Retrieved through the PMC articles route recorded as allowed in this project's source-access ledger. No login, paywall, rate limit, or technical control was bypassed.
